segments.say: Let's go back to where we began, to Nora in her bed with the lamp off and the curtains closed. It's a night much like the first one, tired, quiet and a little uncertain. But something is different. She isn't doing the sums, the clock faces the wall, and her notebook sits on the table with tomorrow's list written in it. She isn't trying to sleep. She's simply lying there, warm and still.

We've covered a great deal tonight, from two clocks and a blocked sleepiness signal, to hidden worries, quiet wake-ups and warm feet. Let's gather it into a few ideas that you can pick up, or put down, as you like.

Keep a steady wake-up time, and give yourself plenty of morning light. Let the evening be dimmer, and move caffeine earlier in the day. Write your worries and tomorrow's plans on paper before bed. Make the room cool, quiet and dark, with warm feet if possible. If you're wide awake for a long time, get up and do something quiet until you feel sleepy. And, above all, bring a little less effort and a little more ease.

show.title: A gentle toolkit
items: Out of bed if wide awake

segments.say: Underneath all of this is the idea that we started with. Sleep depends on two systems, a pressure that builds while you're awake, and a clock that follows the sun. Most of the advice we've heard is a way of helping them to agree. Enough time awake, steady light, and not too much spent on late naps or late caffeine.

The second idea is that the mind matters as much as the body. A worried, effortful, monitoring mind keeps the alert systems on, however tired the body is. Writing things down, turning the clock around, picturing a calm scene, and letting go of the contest are all ways of quietening the watcher, which is the part that tries hardest and helps least.

And one idea may be the kindest of all. Sleep is more forgiving than it feels. A bad night is not a catastrophe, wake-ups are a normal part of the night, and the body has a strong drive to recover. The placebo sleep studies remind us that part of what makes a poor night hard is the story we tell about it, and that story can be changed.

That might be the quiet lesson of tonight. You can't force sleep, but you can make room for it, with light, with timing, with a calmer mind and a gentler attitude. And then, with a bit of patience, you can let it find you.

show.text: You can't force sleep. You can only make room for it.

segments.say: And an honest note. If sleep trouble has lasted for weeks and is affecting your days, if you snore loudly and wake gasping, if your legs are restless, or if low mood or anxiety are weighing on you, please talk to a doctor. These problems are common and many are very treatable, and nothing in tonight's ideas is a substitute for that help.
And now, if you're listening in bed, or on a sofa, or on a train home, let's finish with something slower. There's nothing to do. You can listen, or you can drift.

Wherever you are, let your body be as heavy as it likes. Let your shoulders drop, just a little, and let your jaw soften. There's nowhere you need to be, and nothing that needs to be solved before morning. The day has done its work, and the night has a gentle way of looking after the rest.

Breathe in the way you do when you're not thinking about it. Perhaps a little slower, with a long, quiet breath out, as though you were fogging a window. There's no right way to do it, and no need to count. Just let each breath out be a little longer than the one before, and notice how the body begins to follow.

Rain runs slowly down a dark window pane, and beyond it a distant street lamp glows like a small, patient moon. Inside, a blanket is folded on a chair, and everything in the room has the soft stillness of a night that has nothing left to ask.

show.cap: A window at night with rain

segments.say: Let your attention drift down through your body. Your hands feel warm and heavy. Your feet are a little warmer too, as the blood flows out to the skin, the way it does when the body is getting ready to sleep. Your legs are heavy, and your back is supported, and the bed is holding all of it without any effort from you.

If thoughts come, let them come, and let them go, like clouds passing slowly over a quiet hill. You don't have to follow any of them, and you don't have to push them away. The notebook is on the table, the list is written, and tomorrow will be there in the morning, perfectly able to look after itself.

Somewhere, in a quiet room, there's an imagined woman called Nora, who is sleeping soundly. Her breathing is slow and steady, her hands are warm, and her clock faces the wall. She doesn't know that she's been the star of a long conversation tonight, and she doesn't need to. She's simply asleep, the way all of us are, sooner or later, when we stop trying.

Whether you drift off in the next few minutes, or lie awake a little longer, this quiet is a kind of rest too. Your body is resting, your heart is slow, and the world outside has gone still. You've done everything that anyone can do. The rest is not yours to arrange.

Let yourself notice the room around you, without opening your eyes if they're closed. The air is the temperature it needs to be. The sounds outside are far away, and they're not asking for anything. The bed, the blanket and the pillow are all doing their quiet work, and for the moment, there is nothing else that needs doing.

Think of sleep as a tide. You don't pull it in, and you can't hurry it, and yet it rises on its own, a little at a time, as surely as it has every night of your life. Some nights it's quicker, and some nights it's slower, but it keeps coming back, because that's what tides do, and because your body knows the way.

If there's one last thing to think about, let it be a small, kind one. Something that went a little better than expected today, or something you're looking forward to, however small. And then let that thought go too, and let the quiet take its place, deep, warm and unhurried, with nowhere left to go.

So, from here, there's only one thing left to say. Thank you for spending this long evening with us, for your curiosity and for your patience. Be kind to yourself tonight, and tomorrow. Sleep well, or rest well, and we'll see you next time.

Next time, we'll look at a strange and fascinating question, why being left alone with nothing to do can feel so uncomfortable, that some people would rather do something unpleasant than sit quietly with their thoughts.
